content.intro: Learn sql vs. databases and database management systems through a short explanation, a concept diagram, and a PostgreSQL-oriented example. Focus on the reason for the query or design decision before memorizing syntax.
content.why_it_matters: SQL vs. Databases and Database Management Systems matters because database behavior becomes more reliable when the intended row meaning, data shape, and edge cases are explicit. This lesson follows the SQL curriculum's listed subtopics and calls out PostgreSQL-specific behavior when it matters.

content_blocks.title: The core idea
content_blocks.text: SQL vs. Databases and Database Management Systems gives you the vocabulary to ask for a result without scripting every low-level retrieval step. SQL statements describe the data or operation; the database engine parses, plans, and executes them.

content_blocks.title: Apply the idea
content_blocks.text: Start with the subtopics: SQL vs. a database, SQL vs. a database management system (DBMS), Database server vs. database client, Database engine vs. SQL interface. Define the result you expect, run or inspect the small example in your own disposable PostgreSQL lab, and change one assumption at a time. The embedded lesson editor is a demonstration shell: the current project shows the sample expected output and does not execute arbitrary SQL on the server.

items.title: SQL vs. a database
items.text: SQL vs. a database helps you build a mental model of SQL as a declarative language for relational data, and distinguish the language from the database engine that executes it. content_blocks.code: SELECT current_database() AS database_name, current_user AS database_role;
content_blocks.expected_output: The result identifies the current PostgreSQL database and role; it does not identify the SQL language itself.

Do not use production credentials or a production database. Some specialist examples require optional extensions or a specific PostgreSQL version, as stated in the lesson. The CodeLeaf lesson Run button in this scaffold only previews the documented expected output; it is not a SQL execution service.
content_blocks.reset_steps: For queries, restore the original text and compare results. For statements that change data, use the transaction and rollback shown in the example, or recreate the disposable lab from the included setup instructions. Do not reset production data.

content_blocks.title: Remember
content_blocks.text: SQL correctness depends on data shape, constraints, NULL behavior, row counts, and the target database dialect—not just whether a statement parses.

content.task: Try it yourself: demonstrate sql vs. databases and database management systems using the sample schema. State what each returned row represents, test one edge case related to the lesson, and record the result.
task_acceptance_criteria: The query or design example matches the lesson's intended behavior.
The expected row grain and relevant NULL, duplicate, boundary, or permission behavior are explained.
The test is performed only in the local disposable lab, or clearly marked as a static inspection when a real runner is unavailable.
hints: Begin with the subtopic sql vs. a database and write down the result you expect.
Use the smallest valid example; verify table and column names before adding complexity.
Inspect one edge case: missing values, duplicate matches, tied sort values, a constraint violation, or an engine-specific syntax difference.

common_mistakes.problem: Assuming a query is correct because it returns some rows.
common_mistakes.why: A result can omit valid records, multiply joined rows, mishandle NULLs, or rely on a non-deterministic order.
common_mistakes.fix: Check the expected row grain, add targeted edge cases, and use a stable tie-breaker whenever order or pagination matters.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying PostgreSQL syntax into another SQL engine without checking support.
common_mistakes.why: PostgreSQL, MySQL, SQLite, SQL Server, and Oracle differ in types, functions, row limits, procedural features, and transaction behavior.
common_mistakes.fix: Label the target engine/version and verify the relevant official reference before adapting the query.

common_mistakes.problem: Testing with production data or credentials.
common_mistakes.why: Practice statements can change rows or expose sensitive information if run against the wrong connection.
common_mistakes.fix: Use a dedicated disposable lab, check current_database() and current_user, and review all changes before committing.
